title: The Gillyweed Accord
logline: You are Counsel, retained by the Cetus River Commission. Three neighbouring States around the Cetus river basin are fighting over Gillyweed, a medicinal algae running dry in their shared rivers. Two of them signed a Convention to save it; the third never did, and keeps extracting. Tonight the Tribunal sits. Opposing counsel for the third State has one letter and three arguments. You have the file, three rounds of examination, and the sources of international law to win the river back.
learning_goal: By the end, the player can: 1. State the classical list of sources in Article 38(1) ICJ Statute — treaties, custom, general principles, and (as subsidiary means) judicial decisions and teachings — and separate PRIMARY, law-creating sources from SECONDARY, law-identifying ones [L2 p.10], [T2 p.3]. 2. Apply the VCLT's rules on consent to be bound (signature, ratification, accession — the "wheel of consent"), entry into force, and third-State non-binding (pacta tertiis) to decide who is actually a party to a treaty [L2 p.12-15], [WA2 p.5-8]. 3. Apply the two-element test for customary international law — state practice (consistency, duration, generality) plus opinio juris — independently of any treaty, since custom binds all States including non-parties [L2 p.17-24], [T2 p.5-6], [WA2 p.10-11]. 4. Correctly state and correctly LIMIT the persistent objector rule: it only ever blocks an emerging rule that a State has consistently and openly opposed from the outset; it cannot be raised against an already-settled rule, cannot be claimed by new States against pre-existing custom, and never works against jus cogens [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1]. 5. Avoid the "typical error" of collapsing the different sources into one another — e.g. using the CIL "specially affected States" test to decide whether a treaty has entered into force, or treating a judicial decision as itself a freestanding source rather than subsidiary evidence [L2 p.25], [L2 p.30], [T2 p.3], [WA2 p.2].

quiz.question: Uras signed the CPG on 1 Nov 2020 and ratified on 1 May 2021. Anares signed the same day and ratified on 1 March 2022. Gont, which never negotiated or signed the CPG, sent a diplomatic note in January 2024 saying only that it "intends to sign." Art. 11(1) CPG: the Convention enters into force 30 days after the second ratification. Art. 10 CPG: open for accession by any State described in Art. 8 (all Cetus-region States). Which argument do you make?

options.text: The CPG entered into force for Uras and Anares on 31 March 2022, 30 days after Anares's ratification (Art. 11(1) CPG, Art. 24 VCLT). Gont is a third State: a mere notification of intention creates no obligation (Art. 34 VCLT, pacta tertiis). Gont could still become bound, either by signing and later ratifying (Arts. 8 CPG, 12 and 14 VCLT) or by acceding directly (Art. 10 CPG, Art. 15 VCLT), since accession is exactly the route by which a State that did not negotiate a treaty may join it.
The CPG already binds Gont, because once a regional convention like the CPG is in force it binds every State in the region, whether or not that State ever consented.
options.story: Tavita doesn't even rise. "Counsel is citing a rule that doesn't exist." Nnamdi strikes the argument from the record.
options.teaching: A treaty binds only States that consented to be bound; it creates no obligation for third States without their consent (Art. 34 VCLT, pacta tertiis) [WA2 p.7]. Regional scope is not a substitute for consent.

options.text: Gont can never become a party to the CPG, because only the States that negotiated and signed the original text may be bound by it.
options.story: Tavita smiles for the first time: "Then Gont will simply accede tomorrow morning, Your Honour — Counsel has just told this Tribunal it cannot stop us."
options.teaching: Accession under Art. 15 VCLT (here, also Art. 10 CPG) exists exactly to let a State that never negotiated or signed a treaty join it later. Confusing "not an original party" with "can never be a party" is the error this rule is built to prevent [WA2 p.5], [WD2 p.1].

options.text: The CPG has not entered into force at all, because Gont — clearly a "specially affected State" for Gillyweed — has not yet ratified it, and a treaty needs the specially affected States on board before it can take effect.
options.story: Nnamdi cuts in before Tavita can. "Counsel, that test belongs to customary law. This is a ledger, not a State-practice survey." Halvorsen's ledger stays open to 31 March 2022 regardless.
options.teaching: "Specially affected States" is part of the customary international law test (see Round 2) — it has nothing to do with when a treaty enters into force, which is governed solely by the treaty's own entry-into-force clause and Art. 24 VCLT [L2 p.20-21], [L2 p.25]. Mixing up the tests for different sources is exactly the "typical error" this unit warns against [L2 p.25], [T2 p.3].

irac.rule: a treaty enters into force as it itself provides (Art. 24 VCLT) and binds its parties under pacta sunt servanda (Art. 26 VCLT) [L2 p.12]; it creates no obligation for a third State without consent (Art. 34 VCLT) [WA2 p.7]; Gont's letter is only a notification of intention, so nothing binds it yet, but Arts. 8/10 CPG with Arts. 12, 14 and 15 VCLT leave signature-plus-ratification and accession both open to it precisely because it was not an original party [WA2 p.5], [WD2 p.1].
irac.application: a treaty enters into force as it itself provides (Art. 24 VCLT) and binds its parties under pacta sunt servanda (Art. 26 VCLT) [L2 p.12]; it creates no obligation for a third State without consent (Art. 34 VCLT) [WA2 p.7]; Gont's letter is only a notification of intention, so nothing binds it yet, but Arts. 8/10 CPG with Arts. 12, 14 and 15 VCLT leave signature-plus-ratification and accession both open to it precisely because it was not an original party [WA2 p.5], [WD2 p.1].
irac.conclusion: "The Convention bound its two ratifying parties on 31 March 2022; it binds Gont in no respect, and Gont has walked through neither door that would change that."

quiz.question: Gont has not signed, ratified, or acceded to the CPG. Independently of the Convention, is Gont bound by a customary rule requiring it not to cause transboundary harm to Uras's and Anares's shared rivers?

options.text: Yes. The rule satisfies both elements of the customary-law test. State practice: consistently formulated for over 80 years since the 1941 Trail Smelter arbitration, restated in the Stockholm Declaration (1972, Principle 21) and the Rio Declaration (1992, Principles 14-15), and incorporated into near-universal treaties such as the UNFCCC (198 parties) — satisfying consistency, duration and generality. Opinio juris: the ICJ's 1996 Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion confirmed the obligation is "part of the corpus of international law," and declarations adopted with broad support can themselves be evidence of that legal conviction. Because custom binds all States, not only treaty parties, it binds Gont regardless of the CPG.
No. Gont has not signed the CPG, so it has no obligation of any kind concerning Gillyweed or the rivers until it does.
options.story: Tavita spreads his hands: "Then we are done, Your Honour — my client signed nothing." Ada's grip on the laminated card tightens.
options.teaching: This treats the treaty as the only possible source of Gont's obligations. Customary international law arises independently of any treaty and binds all States, including non-parties [L2 p.17], [T2 p.5]. The CPG's silence about Gont says nothing about whether custom already binds it.

options.text: No. The Stockholm and Rio Declarations are non-binding soft law, so they cannot support any legal obligation on Gont.
options.story: Counsel dismisses the declarations outright; Tavita seizes the opening: "Counsel just conceded my client's entire defence."
options.teaching: Correct that Stockholm and Rio are not binding in themselves — but wrong to conclude they are legally irrelevant. Soft law is admissible evidence of State practice and of opinio juris, and can help a rule "crystallise" into custom [L2 p.31], [WD2 p.1].

options.text: Yes, but only because the ICJ's Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion is itself a binding source of law under Article 38 that directly obliges Gont.
options.story: Tavita: "Since when does an advisory opinion in a case my client was never party to bind my client?" Nnamdi's expression sours.
options.teaching: Judicial decisions are a SECONDARY, subsidiary means for determining what the law is (Art. 38(1)(d) ICJ Statute); they identify or clarify existing law rather than creating it, and the ICJ is not even bound by its own past decisions [L2 p.30], [T2 p.3]. The Advisory Opinion is evidence of the customary rule, not itself the source binding Gont.

irac.rule: Article 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute defines custom as "evidence of a general practice accepted as law" [T2 p.3]; it requires State practice (consistency, duration, generality — with specially affected States particularly relevant) plus opinio juris, a belief the practice is legally required, not mere courtesy [L2 p.17-21], [T2 p.5-6]; unlike a treaty, custom binds all States [L2 p.17]. Here, the Stockholm/Rio Declarations, the 1941 Trail Smelter arbitration, and the near-universal UNFCCC establish State practice, and the ICJ's 1996 Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion supplies direct evidence of opinio juris [WA2 p.10-11]. The rule therefore binds Gont regardless of the CPG.
irac.application: Article 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute defines custom as "evidence of a general practice accepted as law" [T2 p.3]; it requires State practice (consistency, duration, generality — with specially affected States particularly relevant) plus opinio juris, a belief the practice is legally required, not mere courtesy [L2 p.17-21], [T2 p.5-6]; unlike a treaty, custom binds all States [L2 p.17]. Here, the Stockholm/Rio Declarations, the 1941 Trail Smelter arbitration, and the near-universal UNFCCC establish State practice, and the ICJ's 1996 Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion supplies direct evidence of opinio juris [WA2 p.10-11]. The rule therefore binds Gont regardless of the CPG.
irac.conclusion: "The Convention was never the only thing standing over that river."

scenes.title: The Objection That Came Too Late
action: Tavita rises for a final argument, unhurried. The Convention folder and a single exhibit sheet headed "CIL — PREVENTION OF TRANSBOUNDARY HARM" sit side by side on Counsel's table, a neon-teal highlighter line under "settled rule."

dialogue.speaker: TAVITA
dialogue.line: Gont has extracted Gillyweed since before this "rule" of theirs existed. We have never accepted it. We object — we have always objected, simply by continuing as we always have.

dialogue.speaker: COUNSEL
dialogue.line: Continuing as you always have is not the same as objecting, Ambassador.

dialogue.speaker: TAVITA
dialogue.line: Then let us try another door. The Convention is a specific arrangement between two States. Ours is the general law of the river. The specific must yield to the general only where it says so — otherwise the general rule cannot reach a State the specific treaty never bound.

dialogue.speaker: ARBITRATOR NNAMDI
dialogue.line: (to Counsel) Does either argument get Gont out of this obligation?

quiz.question: Round 2 established that prevention of transboundary harm is a settled rule of customary international law. Gont now argues (1) that it is a persistent objector because it has always extracted Gillyweed without restraint, and (2) that the CPG, as the more specific rule between Uras and Anares, means the general customary rule cannot reach Gont at all. Which argument do you make?

options.text: Neither argument works. The persistent objector rule only ever blocks a rule that is still emerging, and only for a State that has consistently and openly objected to it from the outset — merely continuing pre-existing conduct without articulating an objection is not the same thing, and in any case the rule is already settled (Round 2), so there is nothing left to object to. The lex specialis argument fails for a different reason: lex specialis resolves a conflict between two rules that both apply to the same State; the CPG simply does not apply to Gont at all (it only binds its parties, Art. 34 VCLT), so there is no more specific rule of Gont's to prevail as lex specialis. Gont remains bound by the customary rule.
Gont's persistent-objector argument succeeds: since it has always extracted Gillyweed freely, that ongoing conduct is itself the objection, and the customary rule never bound it.
options.story: Nnamdi's gavel-mic light dims for Gont's side. Cut to the riverbank, water level lower still.
options.teaching: Merely continuing pre-existing behaviour is not the same as consistently and openly objecting to an emerging rule — and once a rule is established, it cannot be objected to at all [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1].

options.text: Gont's persistent-objector argument succeeds for a different reason: as a State that only started being relevant to this dispute recently, Gont is automatically exempt from any customary rule that had already formed before then.
options.outcome_title: New to the Dispute, Not New to the Law.
options.story: Nnamdi raises an eyebrow: "The river has been there longer than Gont's objection."
options.teaching: New States are bound by existing customary international law — there is no "fresh start" exception [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1].

options.text: Neither argument matters, because prevention of transboundary harm is a jus cogens norm, so the Tribunal must rule against Gont regardless of anything Gont has argued about timing or objection.
options.story: Counsel wins the point but calls the rule jus cogens; Nnamdi corrects the record for the transcript: "Let it be noted this Tribunal made no such finding."
options.teaching: Jus cogens is reserved for peremptory norms such as the prohibitions of genocide, torture, slavery and aggression (Art. 53 VCLT) [L2 p.31], [T2 p.9]; nothing in this record supports labelling prevention of transboundary harm as jus cogens, and mislabelling an ordinary customary rule this way is itself a common exam error.

irac.rule: a State may avoid an EMERGING customary rule only by persistently and openly objecting to it from the outset (illustrated by the Fisheries Case, where a proposed rule was held "inapplicable as against Norway inasmuch as she has always opposed it") [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1] — but it only applies to a still-emerging rule, never once the rule is established, and new States get no fresh chance to object [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1]. Lex specialis resolves conflicts between rules binding the same State; it cannot let one source exempt a State that a different source never bound in the first place [L2 p.25], [WA2 p.2-3].
irac.application: a State may avoid an EMERGING customary rule only by persistently and openly objecting to it from the outset (illustrated by the Fisheries Case, where a proposed rule was held "inapplicable as against Norway inasmuch as she has always opposed it") [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1] — but it only applies to a still-emerging rule, never once the rule is established, and new States get no fresh chance to object [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1]. Lex specialis resolves conflicts between rules binding the same State; it cannot let one source exempt a State that a different source never bound in the first place [L2 p.25], [WA2 p.2-3].
irac.conclusion: "Silence dressed up as habit is not an objection, Ambassador, and a specific treaty cannot excuse a State it never bound."

case_file: Parties: Uras, Anares (CPG parties) v. Gont (non-party, letter of intention only)
CPG: signed 1 Nov 2020 (Uras, Anares); ratified 1 May 2021 (Uras), 1 Mar 2022 (Anares)
Art. 8 CPG: open for signature by Cetus-region States · Art. 10 CPG: open for accession · Art. 11(1) CPG: enters into force 30 days after 2nd ratification/accession
Gont: letter of intention, Jan 2024 — no signature, no ratification, no accession

irac.issue: Is Gont bound, under any source of international law, to stop unrestrained Gillyweed extraction from the Cetus rivers? [WS2 p.2-4]
irac.rule: A treaty binds only States that consented to be bound (Arts. 24, 26, 34 VCLT); custom binds all States once its two elements — State practice and opinio juris — are shown (Art. 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute; North Sea Continental Shelf, para. 77) [L2 p.12], [WA2 p.7], [T2 p.3], [L2 p.19]. A State can escape only an emerging custom, and only by consistent, open objection from the outset; it cannot escape a settled rule this way, and a treaty that never bound it cannot displace a custom that does, since lex specialis only resolves conflicts between rules binding the same State [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1], [L2 p.25], [WA2 p.2-3].
irac.application: Round 1: the CPG binds Uras and Anares from 31 March 2022; it does not bind Gont, whose letter is a mere notification of intention (Art. 34 VCLT), though accession or signature-plus-ratification remain open to it [WA2 p.5-7]. Round 2: independently of the CPG, the principle of prevention of transboundary harm satisfies both elements of the CIL test — consistent, long-standing, near-universal State practice (Trail Smelter, Stockholm, Rio, UNFCCC) and opinio juris confirmed by the ICJ's 1996 Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion — and therefore binds Gont regardless of the treaty [WA2 p.10-11]. Round 3: Gont's persistent-objector defence fails, because continuing pre-existing conduct is not an open objection and the rule is already settled; its lex specialis defence fails, because the CPG never bound Gont in the first place, leaving nothing for lex specialis to displace [T2 p.6], [WD2 p.1], [WA2 p.2-3].
irac.conclusion: Gont is bound by customary international law to prevent transboundary harm to the shared rivers, independently of and regardless of the CPG, and neither of its defences relieves it of that obligation [WA2 p.11], [T2 p.6].

verdict.takeaway: On the exam: a treaty only ever binds its parties — check custom before you assume a non-party walks free.

checks.claim: Article 38(1) ICJ Statute lists treaties, custom, general principles, and (as subsidiary means) judicial decisions and teachings
Primary sources (treaties, custom, general principles) create law; secondary/subsidiary sources (judicial decisions, teachings) identify or clarify it
Article 2(1)(a) VCLT: definition of a treaty (written, between States, governed by international law, one or more instruments)
Full powers: Arts. 6-7 VCLT; Heads of State/Government/Foreign Ministers represent the State without full powers
"Wheel of consent": signature (Art. 12 VCLT), signature + ratification (Art. 14 VCLT), accession (Art. 15 VCLT), other means (Art. 11 VCLT)
Art. 18 VCLT: interim obligation not to defeat a treaty's object and purpose, after signature or after consent pending entry into force
Art. 24 VCLT: a treaty enters into force as it provides; Art. 26 VCLT: pacta sunt servanda
Art. 34 VCLT: pacta tertiis — a treaty creates no obligation for a third State without its consent
Fictional case facts: Uras/Anares/Gont, CPG signature and ratification dates, Gont's January 2024 letter of intention, Arts. 8/10/11 CPG
CPG entry into force for Uras and Anares on 31 March 2022 (30 days after the second ratification)
Accession (Art. 15 VCLT / Art. 10 CPG) exists precisely to let a non-negotiating State later join a treaty
Art. 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute: custom is "evidence of a general practice accepted as law"
Two-element test for CIL: state practice (objective) + opinio juris (subjective), both required (North Sea Continental Shelf, para. 77)
State practice sub-elements: consistency, duration, generality; "specially affected States" particularly relevant (North Sea, para. 74)
Opinio juris = belief the practice is legally required, distinguished from courtesy/political expediency (Lotus; Asylum case)
CIL binds all States, including non-parties to any treaty on the same subject — unlike a treaty, which binds only its parties
Stockholm Declaration 1972 (Principle 21) and Rio Declaration 1992 (Principles 14-15) as state-practice evidence; UNFCCC's 198 parties
ICJ Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion (1996): the prevention obligation is "part of the corpus of international law"
Soft law (e.g. UNGA-type declarations) is not itself binding but can be evidence of state practice or of crystallising opinio juris
Judicial decisions are a subsidiary/secondary means of determining law, not themselves a freestanding source; the ICJ is not bound by its own precedent
Persistent objector rule: a State may avoid an emerging rule by persistently, openly objecting to it from the outset (Fisheries Case, Norway)
Limits of the persistent objector rule: only for emerging rules, not once settled; new States are bound by existing CIL; never against jus cogens

Lex specialis and lex posterior as conflict rules between sources of equal rank; jus cogens (Art. 53 VCLT) and Art. 103 UN Charter as the exceptions to the otherwise horizontal, non-hierarchical system
Lex specialis concerns specificity between rules binding the same State, not a hierarchy between source-types, and does not let a rule exempt a State a different source never bound
Jus cogens examples: prohibition of genocide, torture, slavery, aggression (Art. 53 VCLT)
Exam format: 8 multiple-choice questions (4 international law, 4 EU law) plus one hypothetical case per part, each with sub-questions
International Law MCQs use a 4-option (a-d) format
IRAC (issue, rule, application, conclusion) is the required format for WG assignments and, by extension, exam hypothetical-case answers
